Motlanthe is expected to hold the presidency until elections scheduled for the spring of next year. ANC President Jacob Zuma is broadly predicted to win that vote.

The ANC called on Mbeki to resign earlier this month, after a judge dismissed corruption, fraud and racketeering charges against Zuma, Mbeki’s leading political rival. The judge ruled that the case was invalid and alleged political interference by Mbeki’s administration.

In Sunday’s televised announcement, Mbeki reflected on his record after nearly a decade as president. CNN also highlighted the importance of Mbeki “falling on the sword.”

“I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all,” he said.

Mbeki credited his administration with overseeing the longest stretch of continuous economic expansion in South African history and with providing unprecedented assistance to impoverished citizens. At the same time, he acknowledged that the country would continue to confront economic difficulties, corruption and crime. Without identifying his successor, he also expressed confidence in the person who would next lead South Africa.

Gwede Mantashe, the ANC’s secretary-general, said Saturday that the party had asked Mbeki—an ANC member since his teenage years—to leave before completing his term and that Mbeki had accepted the request. Mantashe said the decision was taken on behalf of South Africans to preserve national stability and keep the ANC movement united and secure.

Zuma replaced Mbeki as ANC president last year. The criminal case against him had previously been dismissed in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority later filed charges again. Judge Chris Nicholson did not determine whether Zuma was guilty or innocent, meaning prosecutors could charge him once more.

Political analysts considered another prosecution unlikely because Zuma enjoyed substantial support, especially among trade unions and the Communist Party. Zuma denied wrongdoing, arguing that the proceedings were politically driven and had damaged his prospects of becoming the ANC’s presidential candidate.

Had he been convicted of taking bribes from a company awarded a contract in a multibillion-dollar weapons deal, Zuma could have received a prison sentence of at least 15 years. He was also accused of maintaining a corrupt association with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik. Shaik is serving a 15-year prison term for seeking bribes on Zuma’s behalf and exploiting Zuma’s political power to advance his own business interests.

# South Africa’s deputy president, 10 ministers resign after Mbeki exit

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa — September 23, 2008** — South African Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and 10 Cabinet ministers submitted their resignations Tuesday, deepening political uncertainty after President Thabo Mbeki agreed to step down.

The resignations are expected to take effect when Mbeki formally leaves office Thursday, the presidency said. They followed the ruling African National Congress’ decision to recall Mbeki before the end of his second term.

Among those resigning was Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, whose decade-long stewardship of Africa’s largest economy had reassured investors. News of his departure briefly rattled financial markets and weakened the rand, although officials said Manuel was willing to serve in the next administration if asked.

Other departing ministers included several longtime Mbeki allies, raising concerns that the president’s forced exit could trigger a broader split within the ANC.

Mbeki announced his resignation Sunday after accepting the party’s demand that he leave office. The move came amid an escalating power struggle with ANC leader Jacob Zuma, whom Mbeki dismissed as deputy president in 2005.

The ANC acted after a judge suggested there may have been political interference in the corruption case against Zuma. Mbeki denied interfering in the prosecution.

Parliament was expected to elect ANC deputy leader Kgalema Motlanthe as interim president. Motlanthe would lead the government until national elections expected in 2009, when Zuma was widely anticipated to become the ANC’s presidential candidate.

The presidency sought to calm fears that the wave of resignations would disrupt government operations, saying the outgoing officials would remain in their posts until the transfer of power.

Mlambo-Ngcuka, who replaced Zuma as deputy president, had been closely associated with Mbeki’s administration. Her resignation had been widely expected once the president announced he would step down.

The departures marked one of the most significant political upheavals in South Africa since the end of apartheid in 1994. The ANC had governed with commanding parliamentary majorities, but tensions between Mbeki’s supporters and Zuma’s allies threatened the party’s long-standing unity.

Mbeki, who succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999, had been due to remain president until the 2009 election. His early departure brought an abrupt end to nearly a decade in office and set the stage for a rapid transition of power.

counterfactuals.output:
In September 2008, South Africa entered a major political crisis when the African National Congress’s national executive committee “recalled” President Thabo Mbeki, effectively forcing him to resign about seven months before his term ended. The move reflected the ANC’s deep split between Mbeki and supporters of Jacob Zuma, who had defeated him for the party leadership in December 2007.

The immediate trigger was a High Court ruling that invalidated the corruption prosecution of Zuma on procedural grounds. Judge Chris Nicholson also suggested that political interference—potentially involving Mbeki’s government—had influenced the decision to charge Zuma. Although those broader findings were later rejected on appeal, the ANC used the ruling to justify removing Mbeki. Mbeki denied interfering and resigned while insisting that the allegations were unfounded.

His departure prompted a wave of Cabinet resignations, including Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and several ministers and deputy ministers. Finance Minister Trevor Manuel also submitted his resignation, unsettling financial markets, but agreed to remain in office under the new administration. The resignations exposed the scale of the ANC’s internal conflict and raised fears of governmental instability; some Mbeki allies later helped form the breakaway Congress of the People, or COPE.

Parliament then elected ANC deputy president Kgalema Motlanthe as South Africa’s president on 25 September 2008. Motlanthe was widely viewed as a caretaker and compromise figure whose job was to stabilize the government until the 2009 election, when Zuma was expected to become president.

Zuma’s legal troubles remained central to the crisis. He faced charges of corruption, fraud, racketeering and money laundering connected to South Africa’s arms deal and his relationship with businessman Schabir Shaik. The September 2008 judgment did not acquit Zuma on the merits; it set aside the prosecution because proper procedures had not been followed. The Supreme Court of Appeal later overturned Nicholson’s ruling and criticized his conclusions about political interference. Nevertheless, prosecutors dropped the charges in April 2009 after recordings—the “spy tapes”—indicated political manipulation of the timing of the prosecution, clearing Zuma’s path to the presidency.

**BREAKING NEWS | SOUTH AFRICA**

# Mbeki resigns after ANC recall; senior ministers follow as Motlanthe prepares to take power

**CAPE TOWN, Sept. 23, 2008** — South Africa is preparing for a rapid transfer of power after President Thabo Mbeki agreed to resign at the request of the governing African National Congress, ending his presidency months before his second term was due to expire.

Mbeki’s departure follows a decisive intervention by the ANC’s National Executive Committee, which voted to “recall” him after a court ruling raised questions about possible political interference in the prosecution of ANC president Jacob Zuma. Mbeki has denied interfering in the case.

His resignation has also triggered a broader government shake-up. Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and a group of senior ministers and deputy ministers have submitted their resignations, although some—including Finance Minister Trevor Manuel—are expected to remain in government under the incoming president.

ANC deputy president Kgalema Motlanthe is expected to be elected by Parliament as South Africa’s interim president, serving until elections in 2009.

## Why Mbeki resigned

Mbeki did not leave because of a parliamentary no-confidence vote or an electoral defeat. He resigned after the ANC leadership formally asked him to step down.

The immediate catalyst was a Sept. 12 ruling by High Court Judge Chris Nicholson in the corruption case against Zuma. Nicholson set aside the decision to prosecute Zuma on procedural grounds and said the circumstances supported an inference of political involvement in the handling of the case. His judgment referred to the political struggle between Zuma and Mbeki and raised the possibility that prosecutorial decisions had been influenced by senior figures in government.

The ruling gave Zuma’s allies fresh ammunition in their long-running claim that the corruption case had been manipulated to block his political rise. Mbeki rejected allegations that he or his Cabinet had improperly influenced prosecutors and subsequently sought to contest the findings that implicated him.

Nicholson’s judgment did not establish through a trial that Mbeki had personally directed the prosecution. Its broader comments about political interference would remain contested and were later subject to appeal. Nevertheless, the ruling had an immediate and devastating political effect.

Zuma had already defeated Mbeki for the ANC presidency at the party’s Polokwane conference in December 2007. That left South Africa with two centers of authority: Mbeki remained president of the country, while Zuma controlled the party that held a commanding majority in Parliament.

After the Nicholson ruling, Zuma’s supporters pressed the ANC’s National Executive Committee to remove Mbeki. The committee decided on Sept. 20 to recall him. Although an ANC “recall” has no direct constitutional force, the party’s parliamentary majority meant Mbeki would have faced removal if he refused.

Mbeki announced the following day that he had accepted the party’s decision and would resign in the interests of political stability.

## Which senior officials followed him

The transition widened when the presidency announced the resignations of Deputy President Mlambo-Ngcuka, 10 ministers and three deputy ministers. Among the most prominent were:

- **Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka**, deputy president  
- **Trevor Manuel**, finance minister  
- **Mosiuoa Lekota**, defence minister  
- **Ronnie Kasrils**, intelligence services minister  
- **Essop Pahad**, minister in the presidency  
- **Alec Erwin**, public enterprises minister  
- **Sydney Mufamadi**, provincial and local government minister  
- **Geraldine Fraser-Moleketi**, public service and administration minister  
- **Thoko Didiza**, public works minister  
- **Manto Tshabalala-Msimang**, health minister  
- **Ngconde Balfour**, correctional services minister  

The deputy ministers submitting resignations included:

- **Aziz Pahad**, deputy foreign affairs minister  
- **Jabu Moleketi**, deputy finance minister  
- **Loretta Jacobus**, deputy correctional services minister  

The resignations were not all necessarily acts of rebellion against the ANC or declarations that the officials would refuse to serve the next administration. Some ministers regarded stepping down as the appropriate constitutional and political response to the departure of the president who had appointed them.

Manuel’s resignation caused particular concern because of his importance to economic policy and investor confidence. The ANC moved quickly to indicate that he was willing to continue as finance minister under Motlanthe, limiting fears that the political crisis would disrupt the Treasury or change South Africa’s fiscal direction.

Other departures, particularly those of close Mbeki allies such as Essop Pahad, Lekota and Kasrils, were expected to be permanent.

## How the transition will work

Under South Africa’s Constitution, the National Assembly must elect a new president from among its members after the incumbent’s resignation takes effect.

The expected sequence is:

1. **Mbeki’s resignation becomes effective.**  
   He submits his resignation to the speaker of the National Assembly, creating a vacancy in the presidency.

2. **Parliament convenes to elect a successor.**  
   The chief justice, or another designated judge, presides over the election in the National Assembly.

3. **The ANC nominates Kgalema Motlanthe.**  
   Because the ANC holds a large parliamentary majority, Motlanthe’s election is effectively assured.

4. **Motlanthe is sworn in as president.**  
   Once elected, he takes the constitutional oath and immediately assumes presidential authority.

5. **A new deputy president and Cabinet are appointed.**  
   Motlanthe is expected to appoint National Assembly Speaker Baleka Mbete as deputy president. He will also decide which ministers remain, which are reassigned and who fills the posts left vacant by resignations.

Motlanthe is expected to govern as a caretaker president until the 2009 general election rather than seek to displace Zuma as the ANC’s principal candidate for national leadership.

## Why Zuma is not taking office immediately

Although Zuma is ANC president and the party’s dominant political figure, Motlanthe is the practical choice for the interim presidency.

The Constitution requires the National Assembly to elect the president from among its members. Zuma is not currently an MP, while Motlanthe entered Parliament earlier in 2008 and is eligible for election.

Choosing Motlanthe also allows the ANC to stabilize the government without forcing an immediate Zuma presidency amid continuing legal and political controversy. Motlanthe is widely viewed as a disciplined party administrator with support across competing ANC factions.

## A caretaker government, but not a powerless one

Motlanthe will inherit the full constitutional powers of the presidency. He will not merely be an acting ceremonial figure. He will be able to appoint ministers, oversee government policy, sign legislation and represent South Africa internationally.

Politically, however, his mandate will be transitional. He will be expected to:

- maintain continuity in economic and fiscal policy;
- prevent the Cabinet resignations from disrupting government;
- manage tensions between Mbeki and Zuma supporters;
- prepare the administration for the 2009 election; and
- reassure investors and foreign governments that the transfer of power will remain constitutional.

The ANC has stressed that the change is not a coup and that state institutions will continue to function normally. Yet Mbeki’s removal marks one of the most dramatic political ruptures since the end of apartheid, exposing deep divisions within the movement that has governed South Africa since 1994.

Mbeki, who succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999, will leave office roughly seven months before the expected end of his term. Motlanthe’s installation will complete an unusually swift transition—from an internal ANC decision to the resignation of a sitting head of state and the parliamentary election of his successor in less than a week.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a historical news account of Thabo Mbeki’s 2008 departure from office, covering his achievements, his rivalry with Jacob Zuma, the ANC’s role, and his recent mediation of Zimbabwe’s power-sharing agreement.
counterfactuals.output:
## Mbeki Leaves Office After ANC Recall, Ending a Transformative but Divisive Presidency

**PRETORIA, Sept. 25, 2008** — Thabo Mbeki stepped down as president of South Africa on Thursday after his governing African National Congress ordered him to resign, bringing an abrupt end to nearly a decade in office and closing one of the most consequential chapters of the country’s post-apartheid era.

Parliament elected ANC deputy president Kgalema Motlanthe as caretaker president until national elections expected in 2009. Mbeki had formally submitted his resignation after the ANC’s National Executive Committee announced on Sept. 20 that it had “recalled” him, a decision he said he accepted as a loyal member of the movement.

The recall followed a High Court ruling that raised the possibility of political interference in the corruption prosecution of Jacob Zuma, Mbeki’s former deputy and his chief rival within the ANC. Although Mbeki denied interfering in the case—and the court’s findings were later overturned—the judgment intensified pressure from a party leadership increasingly dominated by Zuma’s supporters.

Mbeki, who succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999, presided over years of sustained economic growth, rising tax revenues and comparatively disciplined fiscal management. His government expanded housing, electricity and social grants, while helping position South Africa as a leading diplomatic and economic power on the continent.

Abroad, Mbeki championed an “African Renaissance,” played a central role in the creation of the African Union and promoted the New Partnership for Africa’s Development. He also invested heavily in African peace initiatives, mediating conflicts in Burundi, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ivory Coast and elsewhere.

His record was nevertheless deeply contested. Critics accused his administration of being remote and overly centralized, while his questioning of the scientific consensus linking HIV to AIDS delayed the broad provision of antiretroviral medicines during one of the country’s gravest public-health crises. His approach to Zimbabwe—often described as “quiet diplomacy”—was also attacked for being too accommodating toward President Robert Mugabe.

Only days before his recall, however, Mbeki secured one of his most prominent diplomatic achievements. On Sept. 15, Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai signed a power-sharing agreement in Harare after negotiations mediated by Mbeki on behalf of the Southern African Development Community. The accord left Mugabe as president, created a prime minister’s post for Tsvangirai and called for a coalition government intended to end months of political violence and economic collapse following Zimbabwe’s disputed elections.

The durability of that agreement remained uncertain, with the rival parties still divided over the allocation of key ministries and executive authority. Even so, it gave Mbeki a final diplomatic success at the moment his political authority at home was collapsing.

The roots of his departure lay in his long struggle with Zuma. Mbeki dismissed Zuma as South Africa’s deputy president in 2005 after Zuma’s financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption in a case that implicated Zuma. Zuma was later charged with corruption and other offenses, but he retained strong support among trade unions, the ANC Youth League, the South African Communist Party and party members who viewed Mbeki’s government as aloof from the poor.

At the ANC’s national conference in Polokwane in December 2007, Zuma defeated Mbeki for the party presidency. From then on, South Africa effectively had two centers of power: Mbeki in the Union Buildings and Zuma at the head of the organization that had placed him there.

The ANC’s decision to recall Mbeki demonstrated the party’s supremacy over a president elected by Parliament on its ticket. It also exposed deep internal divisions. Several ministers and senior officials resigned in solidarity, though some later agreed to remain under Motlanthe to preserve stability.

Mbeki left office with no public confrontation, saying in a televised address that he remained committed to the ANC and to South Africa. His departure was orderly and constitutional, but unmistakably forced—a striking reversal for a leader who had once appeared to dominate both the government and the liberation movement.

His legacy combined economic modernization and continental ambition with political centralization, bitter factional conflict and grave failures over HIV/AIDS. The Zimbabwe agreement offered a final reminder of the influence he wielded across Africa, even as the ANC brought that influence to an end at home.
